Jumps, point jets and smooth division

Exposition and figures by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and exercises: CC0. Supplied programme prerequisites retain their stated licences.

At a corner, successive derivatives record the mismatched one-sided derivatives as point masses and their derivatives. Multiplication by a function vanishing at that point removes some of those terms. We calculate these operations exactly and use them to solve multiplication equations on an arbitrary open interval. A zero of finite order permits division; a zero at which every derivative vanishes obstructs even division of the constant function one.

All distributions are complex-linear. Write and The finite-order estimate and the canonical action on compact tests are Order, positivity and distributional limits, Section 1 and Proposition 1.2. Restriction, local uniqueness, compatible gluing and smooth multiplication are proved in Local data and compatible products, Sections 1–4. The scalar Taylor, cutoff and compactness arguments use the supplied calculus foundations, §§12–13; integration uses the integration foundations, §§15–16.

Two exact earlier proofs will be used. Weak equations and classical functions, Theorem 4.1 and (4.2), proves when the one-sided derivatives through have finite limits and the ordinary -th derivative is integrable near . Its proof integrates by parts on both sides and then iterates. Finite parts of singular powers, Lemma J, proves that a distribution supported at one point is a finite sum of point derivatives, using the finite-order estimate and shrinking Taylor cutoffs.

Smooth multipliers and their zeros

A zero of a smooth complex function has multiplicity if for and . A zero is of infinite order, or flat, if every derivative vanishes there.

Lemma 4 (finite-order zeros are isolated). At a zero of multiplicity , with smooth on an interval about . It is nonzero on a smaller interval. If has no flat zeros on , its zero set is relatively closed and locally finite in .

Proof. Taylor's integral remainder supplies Every derivative passes through this compact integral, proving smoothness; at the integral of the weight is , giving (J18). Continuity makes nonzero nearby, so is the only zero there. The zero set is relatively closed by continuity of . If infinitely many distinct zeros lay in a compact subset of , compactness would give an accumulation point in . It would be a zero by continuity, contradicting its isolation. Thus each compact set meets only finitely many zeros.

Proof: one global solution. We give the gluing explicitly, because arbitrary local solutions need not agree on overlaps. Choose the intervals pairwise disjoint and locally finite, shrinking them so that their closures lie inside the preceding factorization intervals. This can be done as follows. Choose their radii at most one, less than one third the distance from to any other zero, and less than one quarter its distance to a finite endpoint of . A missing endpoint or the absence of other zeros imposes no corresponding bound. Isolation makes any required separation distance positive. Two such intervals are disjoint, since their radii sum to less than two thirds the distance between their centers.

Exercise 6 (advanced) — the kernel at an isolated flat zero. Let and for . Describe , and decide whether is solvable.

Solution. Successive ordinary derivatives off zero are a polynomial in times . Each tends to zero at zero: with , any fixed power is dominated by , as follows from its positive power series. Inductively the zero-extended derivatives are the actual derivatives at zero, since their difference quotients are of the same vanishing form. Thus is smooth and flat at zero.
